claims.text: Balanced incorporation of lightweight elements such as Al, Ti, V, and Nb with small amounts of Cr or Cu produces a homogeneous single-phase lightweight HEA.
Atomic-size mismatch in a homogeneous HEA produces significant lattice strain.
Lattice distortion strengthens HEAs by increasing resistance to deformation.
High mixing entropy stabilizes a uniform disordered solid-solution structure.
Controlled amounts of Cr or Cu facilitate rapid formation of a dense Al2O3/Cr2O3 protective oxide at high temperature.
A dense Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale reduces high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
The protective oxide also mitigates corrosion in saline environments.
The proposed homogeneous, strained microstructure and protective oxide can simultaneously provide low density, high strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance.
A near-equimolar lightweight HEA made by vacuum arc melting or magnetron sputtering under equilibrium processing will form a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Disrupting the optimal elemental balance causes local segregation and intermetallic-phase formation.
Segregation and brittle intermetallic precipitates compromise both mechanical and environmental resistance.
The optimized baseline alloy will have higher yield strength than an alloy in which a promoting element is changed by approximately 15%.
The optimized baseline alloy will have a lower corrosion current density than the compositionally perturbed alloy.
The optimized baseline alloy will oxidize more slowly than the compositionally perturbed alloy at about 900 °C.
The baseline will retain a fine, homogeneous microstructure and develop a uniform dense oxide film, whereas the modified alloy will be phase-inhomogeneous and form a less protective oxide.
Changing a key promoting element by more than approximately 10–20% crosses the threshold for maintaining a single-phase structure.
Composition changes beyond that threshold produce detectable segregation or brittle intermetallic precipitates.
Processing-induced nonequilibrium phases can mask the intended lattice-strain and oxide-formation effects.
